recordings.text: One piece is now hitting several targets at once, which is a fork, and somebody is about to lose something.
This hands the other side a fork, one of their pieces against several targets, which makes for a crowded position.
A different move had a fork in it, several targets for one piece, and nobody played it.
A piece is pinned to its king now, so stepping off that line would expose the king, and it will mostly stay put.
This lets the other side pin a piece to its own king, which puts that piece on a short leash.
Pinning a piece to its king was on offer elsewhere; this move went another direction.
Skewer, then: the front piece is hit, and should it step away, the piece behind is exposed on the same line.
Two pieces sit on one line, and this lets the other side skewer them through the front one, which is simple geometry.
A skewer down one line was available with another move, front piece then back piece, and it was passed up.
The defender comes off the board, so whatever it was guarding may now be loose.
This exposes a defender to capture, and its duties would go unattended.

The enemy king is boxed in by its own pieces, which is the back-rank mate idea, and the king has no room.
The king's own pieces wall it in, and this gives the other side a back-rank mate idea, which is how back ranks go.
There was a back-rank mate idea against a king with no exit square, and it went unused.
A pawn is heading for the last rank to become something bigger, which is the whole point of this move.
One of the other side's pawns now has a road to promotion, so the squares are worth counting.

A discovered attack was sitting in a different move, and it stayed sitting there.

A stronger move threatened two things together, and this one threatens neither.

Another move would have put a rook on a semi-open file, where it has no pawns of its own and the enemy has at least one.

A different move would have isolated a pawn, leaving no friendly pawns on either side of it.
